items.prompt: Zara tests whether warm water dissolves sugar faster than cold water. What does she change?

options.text: the time the sugar takes to dissolve
options.why: This is what she measures.
She should keep this the same.
She should keep this the same to make the test fair.

hints: Look for the one thing that is different between the cups.
Her question is about warm and cold water.
What is warm or cold?
items.explanation: Zara changes the temperature of the water. She measures how long the sugar takes to dissolve and keeps everything else the same.

items.prompt: Ali tests how the height of a ramp changes how far a toy car rolls. Match each part to its job.
pairs: the variables he keeps the same
hints: His question names two things.
He sets one thing himself and finds out the other.
Everything else should not change.
items.explanation: Ali changes the ramp height and measures the distance. He keeps the car and the floor the same to make it fair.

items.prompt: When is a line graph better than a bar chart?

options.why: Colours are separate groups, so a bar chart is better.

options.text: when you measure how something changes over time
when you have only one result
options.why: One result does not need a graph.
Graphs need numbers to plot.

hints: Bar charts compare separate groups.
Line graphs join points with a line.
Which kind of data changes smoothly, like the temperature during a day?
items.explanation: A line graph shows how something changes over time, like the temperature of cooling water. Bar charts compare separate groups.

items.prompt: The table shows hot water cooling down. By how many degrees did it cool in the first 5 minutes?

Temperature (°C)

Cooled by how much means find the difference.
Take the 5-minute temperature away from the start.
items.explanation: The water started at 80 °C and was 64 °C after 5 minutes. 80 take away 64 is 16 degrees.

items.prompt: Look at the cooling results. What pattern do they show?

head: Time (minutes)
Temperature (°C)
figure.alt: Table of hot water cooling: 0 minutes 80 °C, 5 minutes 64 °C, 10 minutes 52 °C, 15 minutes 44 °C, 20 minutes 40 °C.

options.text: The water cooled by the same amount every 5 minutes.
options.why: It cooled by 16, then 12, then 8, then 4 degrees.
The temperature went down, so the water cooled.

options.text: The water cooled quickly at first, then more slowly.
The water stopped cooling after 5 minutes.
options.why: It kept cooling until 20 minutes.

hints: Work out how much it cooled in each 5 minutes.
Compare the first drop with the last drop.
Are the drops getting bigger or smaller?
items.explanation: The drops were 16, 12, 8 and then 4 degrees. The water cooled quickly at first and then more slowly.

solution.say: Find each drop: 80 to 64, 64 to 52, 52 to 44, 44 to 40.
Each drop is smaller than the one before.
So the water cooled fast at first, then slowly.

items.prompt: Use the cooling results. The room is 28 °C. Which is the best prediction for 25 minutes?

head: Time (minutes)
Temperature (°C)
figure.alt: Table of hot water cooling: 0 minutes 80 °C, 5 minutes 64 °C, 10 minutes 52 °C, 15 minutes 44 °C, 20 minutes 40 °C.

options.why: Water cannot cool below the room temperature of 28 °C.
The water was already 40 °C at 20 minutes, and it does not warm up again.
Water does not warm up again by itself.

hints: The water keeps cooling, but more slowly.
The last drop in 5 minutes was 4 degrees.
The next drop should be smaller than that.
items.explanation: The drops are getting smaller, and the last one was 4 degrees. The next drop should be a little smaller, so about 38 °C is the best prediction.

items.prompt: Plants were given different amounts of water each day. Which conclusion matches the results?

figure.alt: Bar chart of plant height after 3 weeks: 0 ml of water 2 cm, 25 ml 9 cm, 50 ml 14 cm, 100 ml 6 cm.

options.text: The more water, the taller the plant.
options.why: The 100 ml plant was shorter than the 50 ml plant.
The heights were very different, from 2 cm to 14 cm.

options.text: Plants grow best with no water.
options.why: The plant with no water grew least.

options.text: 50 ml grew the tallest plant, and 100 ml grew less.

hints: Find the tallest bar.
Look at what happened after that amount.
Did more water always mean more growth?
items.explanation: The tallest plant had 50 ml a day. The plant with 100 ml grew less, so too much water slowed growth as well as too little.

29 cm is close to the other results.

Look for a result that does not fit.

items.explanation: Tries 1, 2 and 4 are all about 30 cm. Try 3 is very different, so it is probably a mistake and should be checked.

Read the two columns together, row by row.

items.prompt: On days when more ice creams are sold, more people get sunburnt. Does eating ice cream cause sunburn?

options.text: Yes, because ice cream makes skin burn.
options.why: Ice cream cannot burn skin.

options.text: No, hot sunny weather causes both.
Yes, because both happen on the same days.
options.why: Two things happening together does not mean one causes the other.

options.text: No, because ice cream is cold.
options.why: Being cold is not the reason. Sunny weather causes both.

hints: Think about what kind of day it is when both happen.
Could something else cause both things?
What makes people buy ice cream and also burns skin?
items.explanation: Hot, sunny days make people buy more ice cream and also cause more sunburn. Two things happening together does not prove that one causes the other.

items.prompt: In a fair test, how many things do you change on purpose?

options.why: You change one thing to see what happens.
Changing more than one thing makes it hard to know the cause.
Everything else must stay the same.

hints: Think about finding out the cause.
If you change many things, which one caused it?
Change just one.
items.explanation: A fair test changes one thing only. Then you can tell what caused any difference.

items.prompt: Bean seedlings grew in different amounts of light. How many centimetres taller was the seedling in the sun than the one in the shade?

Read the height of the sun bar.

items.explanation: The sun seedling was 10 cm and the shade seedling was 6 cm. 10 take away 6 is 4 cm.

Do the test and record the results

You plan before you do.
The conclusion comes last.
items.explanation: A fair test starts with a question and a prediction. We plan, do the test and record, then write a conclusion.

She uses a timer to find out the result.

items.prompt: Choose 2 ways to make the results of a test more reliable.

options.text: Use the average of the results

hints: One result could be a mistake.
More results give a better picture.
Averages use several results.
items.explanation: Repeating a test and finding the average reduces the effect of mistakes. Changing two things or testing once makes the results less reliable.

A fair test changes one thing only.

A map does not show amounts.
This is not about the measurements.

hints: The surfaces are separate groups.
Each group has its own amount.
Bars are good for comparing groups.
items.explanation: The surfaces are separate categories, so a bar chart compares them well. A line graph suits measurements that change over time.

items.prompt: Sugar dissolves in cold water in 90 s. It takes 55 s in warm water and 20 s in hot water. Which water dissolves it fastest?

options.why: Cold took the longest.
Warm was quicker than cold but not the quickest.
The times are different.

hints: Look for the smallest time.
Less time means faster.
Compare the three numbers.
items.explanation: Hot water took only 20 seconds, the shortest time. So it dissolves sugar fastest.

items.prompt: In a fair test we change one thing and keep the other things the ___.
hints: Think of the opposite of different.
Everything else must not change.
The word has four letters.
items.explanation: To make a test fair, only one thing changes. All the others stay the same.

items.prompt: True or false: In a fair test, the variable you change is called the independent variable.
hints: Which variable do you decide?
You change it.
It is the one you change.
items.explanation: You choose and change it on purpose, then see what happens to the other variable.

items.prompt: True or false: The thing you measure is the variable you keep the same.
hints: What do you measure?
Does it stay the same?
You measure what changes.
items.explanation: The thing you measure is the dependent variable, because it changes as a result. Variables kept the same are called control variables.

items.prompt: True or false: A line graph is useful for showing how something changes over time.
hints: What does the line show?
Time goes along the bottom.
It shows change.
items.explanation: The line joins points in order, so you can see rises and falls such as temperature through a day.

items.prompt: True or false: A conclusion can say something that your results do not show.
hints: What is a conclusion based on?
Should it match your results?
It must match the evidence.
items.explanation: A conclusion must be backed by the results. Saying more than your evidence shows is not good science.

items.prompt: The thing we measure in a test is the ___ variable.
hints: It depends on what we change.
The changed one is independent.
It starts with d.
items.explanation: The dependent variable is what we measure. It depends on the thing we change.
